## What we asked

Week 4 hands us community detection, and a new network: 1,444 philosophers born before 1900,
linked when one Wikipedia article links to another. Every method on the menu — Louvain,
Infomap, k-cliques, weights, the disparity-filter backbone — comes with its own idea of what a
"group" is. So we asked the uncomfortable version: where do the methods *disagree*, and is
there one philosopher who keeps turning up at the disagreement?

There is, with one caveat we'll get to. It's Aristotle. The rest of this post is the evidence, and there's a
[live explorable](/explorables/philosophers-backbone.qmd) where you can drag the backbone apart
yourself. (Marvel sat this week out. The philosophers are the shared network now.)

## Loading this week's release

Directed, weighted links; we sum both directions into an undirected weighted graph and keep the
giant component (1,374 philosophers, 9,139 links), which is what every number below refers to.

```{python}
import collections
import math

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import networkx as nx
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from infomap import Infomap
from networkx.algorithms.community import k_clique_communities, louvain_communities, modularity
from sklearn.metrics import normalized_mutual_info_score as nmi

%matplotlib inline

nodes = pd.read_csv("data/week4_philosophers_nodes.tsv", sep="\t", comment="#", quoting=3).set_index("node_id")
edges = pd.read_csv("data/week4_philosophers_edges.tsv", sep="\t", comment="#", quoting=3)
name = nodes["name"].to_dict()

directed = nx.DiGraph()
directed.add_weighted_edges_from(
    (r.source, r.target, r.weight) for r in edges.itertuples(index=False) if r.source != r.target
)

und = nx.Graph()
for u, v, w in directed.edges(data="weight"):
    und.add_edge(u, v, weight=w + (und[u][v]["weight"] if und.has_edge(u, v) else 0))

P = und.subgraph(max(nx.connected_components(und), key=len)).copy()
U = list(P.nodes())
directed = directed.subgraph(U).copy()
print(f"{P.number_of_nodes()} philosophers, {P.number_of_edges()} links, max weight {max(w for *_, w in P.edges(data='weight'))}")
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
def labels(part):
    lab = {n: i for i, c in enumerate(part) for n in c}
    return [lab[n] for n in U]


def by_size(part):
    return sorted(part, key=len, reverse=True)


def top_names(community, k=2):
    return ", ".join(name[n] for n in sorted(community, key=lambda n: -P.degree(n))[:k])


def infomap_partition(is_directed=False, weighted=False, seed=1):
    src = directed if is_directed else P
    idx = {n: i for i, n in enumerate(U)}
    im = Infomap(silent=True, seed=seed, num_trials=20, two_level=True, directed=is_directed)
    for u, v, w in src.edges(data="weight"):
        im.add_link(idx[u], idx[v], w if weighted else 1)
    im.run()
    modules = collections.defaultdict(set)
    for leaf in im.tree:
        if leaf.is_leaf:
            modules[leaf.module_id].add(U[leaf.node_id])
    return by_size(list(modules.values()))


def disagreeing(part_a, part_b):
    """Philosophers whose part_b module mostly lives in a *different* part_a community than they do."""
    lab_a = {n: i for i, c in enumerate(part_a) for n in c}
    moved = set()
    for module in part_b:
        home = collections.Counter(lab_a[n] for n in module).most_common(1)[0][0]
        moved |= {n for n in module if lab_a[n] != home}
    return moved
```

## Louvain against Infomap

Louvain maximises modularity: *more internal links than a degree-matched random graph would
give*. Infomap asks a different question: where does a random walker get stuck? On a link graph
of encyclopedia articles those are not obviously the same thing. Ten Louvain seeds against
Infomap's answer, next to how much Louvain disagrees with *itself*:

```{python}
louvain = [by_size(louvain_communities(P, weight=None, seed=s)) for s in range(10)]
infomap = infomap_partition()

louvain_vs_self = [nmi(labels(louvain[i]), labels(louvain[j])) for i in range(10) for j in range(i + 1, 10)]
louvain_vs_infomap = [nmi(labels(p), labels(infomap)) for p in louvain]

print(f"Louvain:  {sorted(len(p) for p in louvain)}  communities across 10 seeds, Q = {np.mean([modularity(P, p, weight=None) for p in louvain]):.3f}")
print(f"Infomap:  {len(infomap)} modules, Q = {modularity(P, infomap, weight=None):.3f}")
print(f"NMI Louvain vs Louvain (seed to seed): {np.mean(louvain_vs_self):.2f}  (range {min(louvain_vs_self):.2f}-{max(louvain_vs_self):.2f})")
print(f"NMI Louvain vs Infomap:                {np.mean(louvain_vs_infomap):.2f}  (range {min(louvain_vs_infomap):.2f}-{max(louvain_vs_infomap):.2f})")
```

Infomap finds 35 modules where Louvain finds 8, and still sits no further from Louvain (0.69)
than Louvain sits from *itself* (0.69). Different seeds of the same algorithm disagree as much
as two different algorithms do. So "Louvain vs Infomap" is mostly a comparison of granularity
plus a lot of seed noise, and the interesting question is which philosophers are on the
wrong side of the noise. Infomap also has knobs, and the agreement depends on which you turn:

```{python}
variants = {
    "undirected, unweighted": (False, False),
    "undirected, weighted": (False, True),
    "directed, unweighted": (True, False),
    "directed, weighted": (True, True),
}
rows = []
for label, (d, w) in variants.items():
    part = infomap_partition(d, w)
    rows.append({
        "Infomap variant": label,
        "modules": len(part),
        "three largest": ", ".join(str(len(c)) for c in part[:3]),
        "NMI vs Louvain": round(np.mean([nmi(labels(p), labels(part)) for p in louvain]), 2),
    })
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("Infomap variant")
```

Using direction and weights pushes Infomap further from Louvain (0.54 for directed and weighted),
which is the right direction: a random walker cares about who cites whom and how hard, and
modularity, as we ran it, doesn't. Now the figure the question asked for, with the
undirected, unweighted variant so Louvain and Infomap see the same graph:

```{python}
#| label: fig-disagree
#| fig-cap: "Left: the philosopher network, coloured by one Louvain run (seed 3); red rings mark philosophers whose Infomap module mostly lives in a different Louvain community. Right: how Louvain's communities (rows) split across Infomap's modules (columns)."
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 6

lou = louvain[3]
lab_lou = {n: i for i, c in enumerate(lou) for n in c}

# layout only: pull same-community pairs together so the communities separate on the page
layout_graph = P.copy()
for u, v in layout_graph.edges():
    layout_graph[u][v]["layout_w"] = 6.0 if lab_lou[u] == lab_lou[v] else 1.0
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
centres = {i: 1.4 * np.array([np.cos(2 * np.pi * i / len(lou)), np.sin(2 * np.pi * i / len(lou))]) for i in range(len(lou))}
start = {n: centres[lab_lou[n]] + 0.3 * rng.standard_normal(2) for n in U}
pos = nx.spring_layout(layout_graph, weight="layout_w", pos=start, seed=7, iterations=150, k=0.12)
moved = disagreeing(lou, infomap)

palette = ["#c8102e", "#4c72b0", "#55a868", "#dd8452", "#8172b3", "#937860", "#da8bc3", "#8c8c8c", "#ccb974", "#64b5cd"]
fig, (ax, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 6), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.15, 1]})

nx.draw_networkx_edges(P, pos, ax=ax, width=0.15, edge_color="#bbbbbb", alpha=0.5)
xy = np.array([pos[n] for n in U])
ax.scatter(xy[:, 0], xy[:, 1], s=[4 + 1.2 * P.degree(n) ** 0.9 for n in U],
           c=[palette[lab_lou[n] % len(palette)] for n in U], linewidths=0, zorder=2)
mv = np.array([pos[n] for n in moved])
ax.scatter(mv[:, 0], mv[:, 1], s=60, facecolors="none", edgecolors="black", linewidths=0.8, zorder=3)
for i, c in enumerate(lou):
    cx, cy = np.median([pos[n] for n in c], axis=0)
    ax.text(cx, cy, top_names(c, 1), fontsize=9, weight="bold", ha="center", va="center",
            bbox={"boxstyle": "round,pad=0.2", "fc": "white", "ec": palette[i % len(palette)], "alpha": 0.85})
ax.set_axis_off()
ax.set_title(f"{len(moved)} of {len(U)} philosophers ({len(moved) / len(U):.0%}) get a different neighbourhood from Infomap", fontsize=10)

inf_top = infomap[:8]
table = np.array([[len(set(lc) & set(ic)) for ic in inf_top] for lc in lou])
im_ = ax2.imshow(np.log10(table + 1), cmap="Reds", aspect="auto")
ax2.set_yticks(range(len(lou)), [f"{top_names(c, 1)} ({len(c)})" for c in lou], fontsize=8)
ax2.set_xticks(range(len(inf_top)), [f"{top_names(c, 1)}\n({len(c)})" for c in inf_top], fontsize=7, rotation=35, ha="right")
for i in range(table.shape[0]):
    for j in range(table.shape[1]):
        if table[i, j] >= 8:
            ax2.text(j, i, table[i, j], ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7, color="white" if table[i, j] > 60 else "black")
ax2.set_xlabel("Infomap module")
ax2.set_ylabel("Louvain community")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The disagreement is not spread evenly. Plato's Louvain community goes 141 of 148 into a
single Infomap module. Aristotle's is shredded: 45 members go to Plato's module, 30 to
Aquinas's, 19 to Descartes's, and only the rest stay put. Louvain drew one line around
"Aristotle and the people near him"; Infomap says the random walker never stays there. It
leaves through Plato, through the scholastics, or through the early moderns.

## Does weighting rewrite the history?

The unweighted graph treats a passing mention like a lifelong obsession. The weight is how
many times one article links to the other, so it is the cheapest available proxy for "this
philosopher matters to that one". Louvain on the weighted graph, same ten seeds:

```{python}
weighted = [by_size(louvain_communities(P, weight="weight", seed=s)) for s in range(10)]
w_vs_u = [nmi(labels(a), labels(b)) for a, b in zip(louvain, weighted)]

print(f"weighted Louvain: {sorted(len(p) for p in weighted)} communities, Q_w = {np.mean([modularity(P, p, weight='weight') for p in weighted]):.3f}")
print(f"NMI weighted vs unweighted (same seed): {np.mean(w_vs_u):.2f}  (range {min(w_vs_u):.2f}-{max(w_vs_u):.2f})")

movers = disagreeing(louvain[3], weighted[3])
degree = dict(P.degree())
strength = dict(P.degree(weight="weight"))
print(f"\n{len(movers)} philosophers ({len(movers) / len(U):.0%}) change community; highest-degree movers:")
lab_w = {n: i for i, c in enumerate(weighted[3]) for n in c}
for n in sorted(movers, key=lambda n: -degree[n])[:8]:
    print(f"  {name[n]:<28} unweighted -> {top_names(louvain[3][lab_lou[n]], 1):<22} weighted -> {top_names(weighted[3][lab_w[n]], 1)}")
```

Weighting moves a quarter of the network (NMI 0.65 against the same seed unweighted), which
is about what a different seed does anyway. What's specific is *who* moves. The whole
Christian cluster that Louvain hangs off Aquinas (Augustine, Jesus, Plotinus, Dante, Luther)
flips into the Plato-and-Aristotle community once repeated links count for more, and Einstein
and Darwin leave Kant's community for Russell's. Heavier links say the scholastics are
Greek philosophy with a different accent.

## Which tradition is Aristotle really in?

Louvain puts him in the community named after him (216 philosophers, alongside Avicenna,
Averroes and Galileo). Count where his 300 neighbours live:

```{python}
def neighbour_communities(who, part):
    lab = {n: i for i, c in enumerate(part) for n in c}
    return collections.Counter(lab[n] for n in P[who]), lab[who]


for who in ["Aristotle", "Plato", "Immanuel_Kant", "Confucius"]:
    counts, home = neighbour_communities(who, louvain[3])
    print(f"{name[who]}: degree {P.degree(who)}, {counts[home] / P.degree(who):.0%} of neighbours in own community "
          f"({', '.join(f'{c} in {top_names(louvain[3][k], 1)}' for k, c in counts.most_common(4))})")

print()
for k in (4, 5, 6):
    cliques = list(k_clique_communities(P, k))
    homes = sorted((len(c) for c in cliques if "Aristotle" in c), reverse=True)
    print(f"k={k}: {len(cliques)} clique communities; Aristotle is in {len(homes)} of them, sizes {homes}")
```

Only a third of Aristotle's 300 neighbours (98) share his community. Plato manages 43%, Kant
56%, Confucius 67%. More of Aristotle's links point at Plato's community (66) and Aquinas's
(56) than you'd expect of a philosopher who supposedly belongs to a third one, and 34 point at
Kant's. The k-clique view agrees from the other side: at k=4 he is inside a single
817-philosopher blob (the giant of the philosopher network, as clique percolation tends to
produce), but at k=5 he belongs to six clique communities and at k=6 to seven. A philosopher
who sits in seven separate tight groups is not in any of them.

```{python}
#| label: fig-aristotle
#| fig-cap: "Aristotle at the centre, his 300 links coloured by the Louvain community of the philosopher at the other end. Only the orange ones are in his own community."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 8

ego, own = "Aristotle", lab_lou["Aristotle"]
groups = collections.defaultdict(list)
for n in P[ego]:
    groups[lab_lou[n]].append(n)
order = sorted(groups, key=lambda k: (k != own, -len(groups[k])))
angles = {}
theta = 0.0
for k in order:
    span = 2 * np.pi * len(groups[k]) / P.degree(ego)
    members = sorted(groups[k], key=lambda n: -P[ego][n]["weight"])
    for i, n in enumerate(members):
        angles[n] = theta + span * (i + 0.5) / len(members)
    groups[k] = members
    theta += span

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 8))
for k in order:
    color = palette[k % len(palette)]
    for n in groups[k]:
        r = 1.0 + 0.02 * (P.degree(n) ** 0.5)
        x, y = r * np.cos(angles[n]), r * np.sin(angles[n])
        ax.plot([0, x], [0, y], color=color, alpha=0.35, linewidth=0.4 + 0.5 * P[ego][n]["weight"])
        ax.scatter(x, y, s=8 + 3 * P.degree(n) ** 0.8, color=color, zorder=3)
    mid = np.mean([angles[n] for n in groups[k]])
    ax.text(1.42 * np.cos(mid), 1.42 * np.sin(mid), f"{top_names(louvain[3][k], 1)}\n{len(groups[k])} links",
            ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9, color=color, weight="bold")
    for n in groups[k][:1]:
        ax.annotate(name[n], (1.0 + 0.02 * P.degree(n) ** 0.5) * np.array([np.cos(angles[n]), np.sin(angles[n])]),
                    fontsize=7, ha="center", xytext=(0, 5), textcoords="offset points")
ax.scatter([0], [0], s=260, color="black", zorder=4)
ax.text(0, -0.13, "Aristotle", ha="center", weight="bold")
ax.set_xlim(-1.7, 1.7)
ax.set_ylim(-1.7, 1.7)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.set_axis_off()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

His own community is the biggest wedge, but not a majority of the ring: Plato's and Aquinas's
wedges together are bigger than it, and Descartes, Kant and Russell each have one too.

## The backbone, and where it snaps

The disparity filter keeps a link only if it carries a suspiciously large share of at least one
endpoint's strength (`alpha`, smaller = stricter). Instead of picking three arbitrary cut-offs,
add links back in order of `alpha` with a union-find and record every merge of two big
components. The biggest one is where the giant component actually breaks.

```{python}
def alpha_of_edges(G):
    """Disparity-filter alpha per undirected edge: the more significant (smaller) of the two endpoint p-values."""
    alpha = {}
    for u, v, w in G.edges(data="weight"):
        p = [(1 - w / G.degree(x, weight="weight")) ** (G.degree(x) - 1) for x in (u, v) if G.degree(x) > 1]
        alpha[(u, v)] = min(p) if p else 1.0
    return alpha


alpha = alpha_of_edges(P)

parent = {n: n for n in U}
size = {n: 1 for n in U}


def find(x):
    while parent[x] != x:
        parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
        x = parent[x]
    return x


merges = []
for (u, v), a in sorted(alpha.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1]):
    ru, rv = find(u), find(v)
    if ru != rv:
        merges.append((a, min(size[ru], size[rv]), max(size[ru], size[rv]), u, v))
        parent[ru] = rv
        size[rv] += size[ru]

a_break, small, large, u, v = max(merges, key=lambda m: m[1])
print(f"Biggest merge: at alpha = {a_break:.4f}, a {small}-philosopher cluster joins a {large}-philosopher one,")
print(f"through the link {name[u]} — {name[v]}")
print("\nNext five biggest merges:")
for a, s, l, u2, v2 in sorted(merges, key=lambda m: -m[1])[1:6]:
    print(f"  alpha = {a:.4f}: {s} joins {l} via {name[u2]} — {name[v2]}")
```

```{python}
def backbone(threshold):
    H = nx.Graph()
    H.add_edges_from(e for e, a in alpha.items() if a < threshold)
    return H


def giant(H):
    return H.subgraph(max(nx.connected_components(H), key=len)).copy()


grid = np.linspace(0.3, 0.005, 120)
curve = [giant(backbone(t)).number_of_nodes() for t in grid]

after_break = a_break * 0.999
before_break = a_break * 1.001
g_before = giant(backbone(before_break))
g_after = giant(backbone(after_break))
shattered = [n for n in g_before if n not in g_after]
print(f"alpha just above break: giant = {g_before.number_of_nodes()} philosophers; just below: {g_after.number_of_nodes()}")

damage = {}
for n in g_before:
    h = g_before.copy()
    h.remove_node(n)
    damage[n] = g_before.number_of_nodes() - 1 - giant(h).number_of_nodes() if h.number_of_nodes() else 0
print("\nRemove one philosopher from the giant component (alpha just above the break) and count who gets stranded:")
for n, d in sorted(damage.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1])[:6]:
    print(f"  {name[n]:<30} strands {d:>3}  (degree in backbone: {g_before.degree(n)})")
```

The sharpest single break is at alpha = 0.047, where Augustine and Malebranche's link joins a
40-philosopher cluster to a 68-philosopher one (a medieval-to-Cartesian bridge, if you squint).
The giant goes from 108 philosophers to 61 across that one link. Ask which *philosopher*
strands the most people at that alpha and the answer is Erasmus (46), then Augustine (42),
Malebranche (39), Descartes (38), and Aristotle fifth at 31. That is not our headline, and we
didn't expect it. The Aristotle–Aquinas link doesn't show up until alpha = 0.031, as a
13-joins-28 merge.

One philosopher is not the same at every alpha, though. Repeat the removal test at every
alpha from 0.20 down to 0.02 and note who strands the most people each time:

```{python}
def most_damaging(G):
    base = G.number_of_nodes()
    hits = {}
    for n in G:
        h = G.copy()
        h.remove_node(n)
        hits[n] = base - 1 - (giant(h).number_of_nodes() if h.number_of_nodes() else 0)
    return max(hits.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1]) + (hits.get(ego, 0),)


sweep = []
for a in np.arange(0.20, 0.019, -0.01):
    g = giant(backbone(a))
    top, stranded, ari = most_damaging(g)
    sweep.append({"alpha": round(a, 2), "giant": g.number_of_nodes(), "top breaker": name[top], "strands": stranded, "Aristotle strands": ari})
sweep = pd.DataFrame(sweep)
print(sweep["top breaker"].value_counts().to_string())
sweep[sweep.alpha <= 0.12].set_index("alpha")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-backbone
#| fig-cap: "The disparity-filter backbone at three values of alpha. Red: the giant component. Black: Aristotle and his backbone links. Left: the giant component's size as alpha tightens, with the break marked."
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 4.6

alphas = [0.2, before_break, after_break]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(13, 4.6), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [0.9, 1, 1, 1]})

ax = axes[0]
ax.plot(grid, curve, color="#c8102e", linewidth=2)
ax.axvline(a_break, color="black", linestyle=":", linewidth=1)
ax.annotate(f"break\nalpha = {a_break:.3f}", (a_break, g_after.number_of_nodes()), xytext=(0.12, 350), fontsize=9,
            arrowprops={"arrowstyle": "->", "linewidth": 0.8})
ax.set_xlabel("alpha (stricter →)")
ax.set_ylabel("giant component size")
ax.invert_xaxis()
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

for ax, a in zip(axes[1:], alphas):
    H = backbone(a)
    G = giant(H)
    nx.draw_networkx_edges(P, pos, ax=ax, width=0.1, edge_color="#e4e4e4")
    nx.draw_networkx_edges(H, pos, ax=ax, width=0.5, edge_color="#999999")
    nx.draw_networkx_edges(G, pos, ax=ax, width=0.9, edge_color="#c8102e")
    aristotle_edges = [(ego, n) for n in H[ego]] if ego in H else []
    nx.draw_networkx_edges(H, pos, ax=ax, edgelist=aristotle_edges, width=1.6, edge_color="black")
    ax.set_title(f"alpha = {a:.4f} · {H.number_of_edges()} links\ngiant component: {G.number_of_nodes()}", fontsize=10)
    ax.set_axis_off()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The sweep decides it. Erasmus's reign lasts one alpha value. Aristotle is the most damaging
single removal at six of nineteen, including every alpha from 0.04 down to 0.02, where the
backbone has shrunk to the ancient-philosophy core and the answer is Aristotle, with
Plato or Socrates a distant second. The break itself is a medieval story, and the last thing standing is
a Greek one.

## What surprised us

That Louvain isn't the odd one out. Its disagreement with Infomap (NMI 0.69) is the size of its
disagreement with its own reruns, so the headline "the methods disagree" turns into "the
methods disagree about the same few people", and those people are Aristotle's neighbours.
Infomap breaks his Louvain community into three; weights fold the medieval Christians into the
Greeks; k-cliques put him in seven groups at once. Only a third of his links stay inside his
own community, which is the lowest of any of the big four we checked.

The part we didn't expect is the backbone. We went in expecting one clean philosopher to
break it, and Aristotle broke it in our first, coarse sweep. Doing it properly, the single
sharpest break is Augustine–Malebranche, with Erasmus as the philosopher who costs the most
there. Aristotle's job is different: he is what the backbone keeps at the very end.
Which one you call "the seam" depends on whether you mean where the network tears first or
what holds until the end, and we'd argue for the second.
